notes: KSČ (Husák) holds ruling slot 4. Biľak/Indra's 'Healthy Forces' sit in 6 as the neo-Stalinist hardliners; the StB is the security power bloc in 7 (0.08); Štrougal's Realists in 13; Dubček's purged reformers in 19; the Revolutionary Youth Movement (HRM) in 5. ČSL moved from MD slot 14 to slot 1 (Christian democracy, has popularity); ČSS in 18 as MD places its successor ČSNS; exile ČSSD in 3; Council of Free Czechoslovakia in 0; Svědectví in 2; Šik's market reformers in 16; Bata in 15; Matica slovenská in 20; exiled HSĽS in 21. The minor Slovak satellite parties (SSO, Strana slobody) are not placed. Slots 8-12 are foreign-student circles (no recognised Muslim community existed in 1970).

0.name: Rada svobodného Československa
0.text:
The Council of Free Czechoslovakia was founded in Washington in 1949 by democratic politicians who fled the communist coup of February 1948, and claims to speak for the captive nation before Western governments. Supported through American Cold War channels and close to Radio Free Europe, it has grown old and quarrelsome, but the flight of tens of thousands after the invasion of August 1968 has brought it new blood.

The Council wants Czechoslovakia restored as a Western-aligned state, with Soviet troops withdrawn, the communists removed from power and a strong provisional authority to oversee the transition, punish collaborators and return confiscated property. Its leverage lies in its Western patrons, émigré networks in America and Europe and its claim to continuity with the pre-1948 republic.

1.name: Československá strana lidová
1.text:
The Czechoslovak People's Party is the Catholic party built up after 1919 by Monsignor Jan Šrámek, which since 1948 has survived as a licensed member of the communist-led National Front. Under the collaborating priest Josef Plojhar it was a docile satellite, but in the spring of 1968 its members ousted him, tens of thousands of believers joined and the party briefly spoke as a genuine Christian democratic voice.

The party seeks religious freedom, the reopening of seminaries and religious orders, Christian education and respect for private farming and small enterprise, within the limits the regime tolerates. Its base is the Catholic countryside of Moravia and its small towns. Its leverage lies in its legal existence, its seats in parliament and its potential as the nucleus of a Christian democratic revival.

2.name: Svědectví
2.text:
Svědectví is the Czech exile quarterly founded in 1956 by the Catholic journalist Pavel Tigrid, who fled after the 1948 coup, and edited from Paris since 1960. Smuggled into Czechoslovakia, it became essential reading for reformers during the Prague Spring, and since the invasion it has opened its pages to the new wave of émigrés and to writers silenced at home.

Svědectví stands for parliamentary democracy, human rights, a market economy and Czechoslovakia's return to Europe, while rejecting the reactionary nostalgia of the old émigré right. It argues that change will come from the regime's own contradictions and the pressure of an informed society. Its leverage lies in ideas, in Tigrid's contacts among Western journalists and politicians and in its influence on dissident intellectuals at home.

3.name: Československá sociální demokracie
3.text:
Czechoslovak Social Democracy, one of the pillars of the interwar republic, was forced into a merger with the communists in June 1948 by its fellow-travelling chairman Zdeněk Fierlinger. Its independent leadership survives in exile in London, linked to the Socialist International. In 1968 veterans in Prague formed a preparatory committee to revive the party, but the communist leadership blocked it even before the invasion, and its activists are now under surveillance.

The party stands for parliamentary democracy, free trade unions, a mixed economy and a welfare state on the Western European model, rejecting both Soviet domination and capitalist restoration. Its base is the memory of older workers and the post-invasion émigrés. Its leverage lies in Western socialist parties and the appeal its name would have in any free election.

4.name: Komunistická strana Československa
4.text:
The Communist Party of Czechoslovakia has ruled since February 1948. In April 1969 Moscow's pressure replaced Alexander Dubček with the Slovak Gustáv Husák, himself a victim of the Stalinist trials, who now presides over 'normalisation': censorship is restored, reformers are being removed from every post and a screening of all members is about to expel or strike off hundreds of thousands. President Ludvík Svoboda and Prime Minister Oldřich Černík lend continuity.

The party proclaims the leading role of the communists, unbreakable friendship with the Soviet Union and the 'temporary' stationing of Soviet troops, and offers citizens a bargain of material security in exchange for political silence. Its base is the apparatus, loyal cadres and the beneficiaries of the purges. Its leverage is total, backed by the Soviet army.

5.name: Hnutí revoluční mládeže
5.text:
The Revolutionary Youth Movement was founded in late 1968 by young radicals, among them Petr Uhl and Petruška Šustrová, who refused to accept the defeat of the Prague Spring. Inspired by the Western New Left, Trotskyism and the Paris revolt of May 1968, it spread leaflets calling for resistance; in December 1969 the security police began arresting its members, and its leaders now await trial.

The movement rejects both Soviet-style bureaucratic socialism and Western capitalism, demanding power for workers' councils, self-management, free trade unions and a revolutionary socialist democracy. It calls the regime a bureaucratic dictatorship serving a foreign occupier. Its base is a few dozen students and young workers, and its leverage lies in courage, contacts with the Western far left and its appeal to a radicalised youth.

6.name: Zdravé síly
6.text:
The Healthy Forces, as Soviet propaganda calls them, are the hardline communists who welcomed the invasion of August 1968. Led by Vasil Biľak and Alois Indra, both among the authors of the letter inviting Soviet intervention, and cheered on by militant old Stalinists such as Josef Jodas and his Libeň group, they now hold key posts in the Presidium, the Central Committee secretariat and the apparatus.

They demand a thorough purge of every reformer, trials of the 'counter-revolutionaries' of 1968, total ideological discipline and the closest integration with the Soviet Union. They regard Husák as too soft and court the Soviet embassy directly. Their leverage lies in Moscow's trust, the People's Militias and the stream of denunciations that fuels the purges.

7.name: Státní bezpečnost
7.text:
State Security, the political police of the Ministry of the Interior, was the terror of the 1950s and was briefly humbled during the Prague Spring, when its crimes were exposed and its archives threatened. Since the invasion it has been purged of reform-minded officers and rebuilt with the help of Soviet KGB advisers, and in August 1969 it helped crush the anniversary demonstrations against the occupation.

The StB sees itself as the shield of socialism and the guarantor of normalisation. It wants unlimited powers of surveillance, informers in every workplace, tight control of foreign travel and exhaustive files on the 'right-wing opportunists' of 1968. Its leverage lies in fear, in compromising material on half the political class and in its direct line to the KGB.

8.name: Kruh imáma Músy
8.text:
The Imam Musa Circle is a handful of Lebanese Shia students in Prague and Bratislava, most of them sent on scholarships arranged by leftist parties, who have found their way back to faith. They take their inspiration from Imam Musa al-Sadr, the Iranian-born cleric of Tyre whose Supreme Islamic Shia Council, constituted in 1969, is giving Lebanon's poorest community a political voice.

The circle preaches a modern, socially engaged Shiism: education, justice for the deprived south, dialogue with Christians and loyalty to a pluralist Lebanon, rejecting both communist atheism and clerical passivity. It keeps a low profile in Czechoslovakia, meeting in student rooms for Muharram commemorations and discussion. Its leverage lies only in the future careers of its members and their ties to Musa al-Sadr's movement.

9.name: Hlas Nadžafu
9.text:
The Voice of Najaf is a tiny clandestine circle of Iraqi and Iranian Shia students in Prague who copy and circulate the letters of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, in exile in Najaf since 1965, and the tracts of the underground Islamic Dawa Party. The Ba'athist assault on the Najaf seminaries in 1969 has hardened their conviction that only clerical leadership can save the faith.

The circle holds that Shia jurists must rule, that the Shah, the Ba'ath and every secular regime are illegitimate, and that Muslims must resist both American imperialism and Soviet atheism. It despises the communist students who dominate the Arab and Iranian student unions in Prague. Hidden from the security police, its leverage lies only in the fervour of its members and their couriers to Najaf.

10.name: Pražská páteční modlitebna
10.text:
Czechoslovakia has had no recognised Muslim community since the small Muslim Religious Community, founded in 1934 by the convert Mohamed Abdullah Brikcius, faded away after the war. What remains is the Prague Friday Prayer Room, an informal gathering of Arab, African and Asian students of the University of 17 November and staff of Muslim embassies, who pray in a rented hall under the eyes of the authorities.

Its prayer leaders, often graduates of al-Azhar or traditional schools at home, preach a quiet, apolitical Sunni Islam of prayer, fasting and good conduct, respectful of their own governments and of Czechoslovak law. They ask only for a mosque, halal food and a Muslim burial plot. Their leverage lies in the goodwill of Arab embassies, which Prague courts for trade and arms deals.

11.name: Studenti osvobození
11.text:
The Students of Liberation are a secretive handful of Jordanian, Palestinian and Syrian students in Prague and Brno who follow Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Party of Liberation founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Sheikh Taqiuddin al-Nabhani. Its pamphlets reach them from party cells among Arab students in West Germany and Austria, carried across the border in student luggage.

The group teaches that the Muslim world must be reunited under a restored caliphate, that all existing Arab states, whether nationalist, monarchist or socialist, are illegitimate, and that capitalism and communism are both systems of unbelief. It scorns the Soviet-backed Arab nationalists whose scholarships brought many students to Czechoslovakia. Watched by the StB and outnumbered by communist students, its leverage lies only in conviction and secrecy.

12.name: Kruh islámské charty
12.text:
The Islamic Charter Circle unites Sudanese students in Czechoslovakia who support Hassan al-Turabi's Islamic Charter Front, the political arm of the Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood, joined by a few Egyptian and Syrian sympathisers of the Brotherhood. Since Jaafar Nimeiry's coup of May 1969 brought communists into government in Khartoum and put al-Turabi in prison, their feud with the Sudanese communist students in Prague has turned bitter.

The circle calls for an Islamic constitution, sharia-based law and a modern Islamic society built through education and lawful political work. It rejects atheist communism and secular Arab socialism and is wary of Western influence. Its leverage lies in its discipline, its student networks across Eastern and Western Europe and its links to the Brotherhood movement at home.

13.name: Realisté
13.text:
The Realists are the pragmatic centre of the party leadership who sided with Gustáv Husák against both the reformers and the ultras in 1969. Their rising figure is Lubomír Štrougal, a former interior minister, now deputy prime minister and head of the party's bureau for the Czech lands, who is expected to take over the federal government; around him gather economists, planners and managers who value order over ideology.

The Realists want a quiet, depoliticised society kept loyal by rising living standards, cheap housing, cars and weekend cottages, administered by competent technocrats rather than zealots. They accept Soviet supremacy as a fact of life but prefer to limit the purges. Their leverage lies in the government machinery, the planning commission and the population's longing for normality.

14.name: Katolická církev v Československu
14.text:
The Catholic Church, the nominal faith of most Czechs and the living faith of most Slovaks, has been crippled since 1950, when the monasteries were dissolved and bishops imprisoned. In 1968 it briefly revived: interned bishops returned, the Greek Catholic Church was legalised again and the Work of Conciliar Renewal rallied reformist clergy and laity. Prague is governed by Bishop František Tomášek as apostolic administrator, while Bishop Felix Davídek's secret church ordains priests underground.

The Church seeks freedom for its seminaries, orders and press, religious education and an end to state supervision of priests, and quietly offers Christian conscience as an alternative to socialist morality. Its strength lies in Slovak and Moravian villages, pilgrimages and the underground networks of the faithful, which normalisation cannot fully reach.

15.name: Baťa
15.text:
The Bata Shoe Organization is the global footwear empire built in Zlín by Tomáš Baťa, the model capitalist of the First Republic. Nationalised in 1945, its home works now operate as Svit in a town renamed Gottwaldov, while the company lives on abroad under his son Thomas J. Bata, who runs dozens of factories and thousands of shops across the non-communist world from Toronto.

The Bata family embodies everything the regime has abolished: private enterprise, managerial efficiency, profit-sharing for workers and Czech commercial genius. A free Czechoslovakia would offer it restitution and a return to its birthplace, and it would bring Western capital, discipline and markets. Its leverage lies in wealth, prestige among older workers of Moravia and influence in Western business and émigré circles.

16.name: Nový ekonomický model
16.text:
The New Economic Model is the reform programme drafted in the 1960s by economists around Ota Šik at the Economic Institute of the Academy of Sciences. Introduced in stages from 1967 and radicalised during the Prague Spring, it sought to replace central commands with prices, profit and competition; Šik, deputy prime minister in 1968, now lives in exile in Switzerland, and his disciples are being removed from ministries and institutes.

The reformers argue that only market mechanisms, enterprise autonomy, freedom for small private business and opening to Western trade can save the Czechoslovak economy from stagnation. They oppose the return to rigid planning under normalisation. Their leverage lies in their expertise, the sympathy of enterprise managers and young economists, and the obvious failures of the command economy.

17.name: TIS – Svaz pro ochranu přírody a krajiny
17.english: TIS – Union for Nature and Landscape Protection
17.native_full: TIS – Svaz pro ochranu přírody a krajiny
17.text:
TIS, the Union for Nature and Landscape Protection, is the association of Czech naturalists and scientists named after the yew tree. With volunteer groups across Bohemia and Moravia it surveys rare species, cares for reserves and educates the public, and in 1969 a sister organisation, the Slovak Union of Nature and Landscape Protectors, was established in Slovakia.

The conservationists are alarmed by the cost of heavy industry: the sulphur-choked forests of the Ore Mountains, the brown-coal mines devouring North Bohemian villages and the poisoned rivers. They call for strict protection of the Krkonoše and Tatra national parks and for environmental limits on planning, without openly challenging the system. Their leverage lies in scientific authority and the public's affection for the countryside.

18.name: Československá strana socialistická
18.text:
The Czechoslovak Socialist Party is the heir of the Czech National Social Party of Edvard Beneš, a leading democratic force of the interwar republic. Since 1948 it has survived as a licensed satellite in the National Front, but in 1968 it revived with tens of thousands of new members under chairman Bohuslav Kučera. Normalisation is now cutting it back to obedience.

The party stands for a humanist, non-Marxist socialism in the tradition of Masaryk and Beneš: social justice, cooperatives, tolerance, civil liberties and national independence, with goodwill towards both East and West. Its base is the Czech urban intelligentsia, officials and small tradesmen. Its leverage lies in its legal status, its daily Svobodné slovo and a name that still evokes the democratic republic.

19.name: Socialismus s lidskou tváří
19.text:
Socialism with a Human Face is the slogan of the Prague Spring and the banner of the purged reform communists. Alexander Dubček, removed as First Secretary in April 1969 and now sent off as ambassador to Turkey, remains its symbol, alongside Josef Smrkovský, the popular former speaker of parliament, and František Kriegel, expelled for refusing to sign the Moscow Protocol. Thousands of reformist officials, journalists and scholars are losing their posts.

The reformers believe in a democratic socialism with freedom of speech, the rule of law, autonomous trade unions, workers' councils and federal equality for Slovaks, loyal to the Warsaw Pact but free from Soviet dictation. Their leverage lies in their enormous popularity, the memory of 1968 and the sympathy of Yugoslav, Italian and other independent communists abroad.

20.name: Matica slovenská
20.text:
Matica slovenská, the national cultural foundation established in 1863 and seated in Martin, is the guardian of Slovak language, literature and identity. In 1968 it rebuilt a mass membership with branches in towns and villages across Slovakia and became a loud voice for the federalisation achieved on 1 January 1969, as well as for grievances against Prague centralism and the demands of the Hungarian minority.

Matica's nationalists champion Slovak equality, Slovak-language culture and investment in Slovakia, and a few look fondly on the wartime Slovak State. They are suspicious of Czech liberals and Hungarians alike, and many see Husák as a Slovak patriot. Their leverage lies in the countryside, the parishes, the local intelligentsia and the regime's need for Slovak support.

21.name: Hlinkova slovenská ľudová strana
21.text:
Hlinka's Slovak People's Party ruled the wartime Slovak State under President Jozef Tiso, a Nazi satellite that deported tens of thousands of its Jews, and was banned in 1945; Tiso was hanged in 1947. Its heirs survive in exile, above all Ferdinand Ďurčanský, Tiso's former foreign minister, whose Slovak Liberation Committee agitates from West Germany, and Slovak émigré associations in Canada, the United States and Argentina.

The exiles call for an independent Catholic Slovakia, authoritarian and corporatist, free from Czechs, communists and Hungarians, and celebrate 14 March 1939 as their national day. They hope to exploit Slovak resentment and Western anti-communism alike. Their leverage is small: a few sympathetic priests at home, émigré money and the lingering nostalgia of some rural Slovaks.

22.name: Československá lidová armáda
22.text:
The Czechoslovak People's Army stayed in its barracks when the Warsaw Pact invaded in August 1968, and now shares the country with the Soviet Central Group of Forces stationed under the treaty of October 1968. Under the Slovak Minister of National Defence, General Martin Dzúr, its officer corps is being screened, and reformist commanders and the military academies' critics of 1968 are being dismissed.

The army is pledged to the Warsaw Pact and the leading role of the party, but its humiliation in 1968 has left many officers bitter and its public prestige low. Purged and reorganised, it is meant to become a reliable pillar of normalisation. Its leverage lies in its weapons, its discipline and the backing of the Soviet commanders, who would decide any crisis.

23.name: Haus Habsburg-Lothringen
23.text:
The House of Habsburg-Lorraine ruled Bohemia, Moravia and the Hungarian crown lands, Slovakia included, until 1918, when the last emperor-king, Charles I, was swept away by the new Czechoslovak republic. His son Otto von Habsburg, head of the house, lives in Bavaria and campaigns tirelessly for a united Europe in the Paneuropean movement, while the family's Czech estates were confiscated long ago.

In Czechoslovakia monarchism survives only among a few aristocrats, some elderly Catholics and émigré legitimists who see the old Danubian monarchy as a lost home of small nations. A Habsburg restoration would stand for Catholic tradition, the rights of nationalities and a Central European federation. Its leverage is symbolic, resting on Otto's European prestige and nostalgia for the pre-1918 order.
